interactions.summary: Jiang distinguishes early infernal sins from deeper ones by arguing that lust, gluttony, greed, and wrath are failures of ego, will, and hope, while violence, fraud, and treachery damage other people's capacity to live well.
A student asks whether ego, free will, and imagination form a spectrum; Jiang agrees and answers by redefining Francesca's lust as a failure of will, not an excess of appetite.

Jiang proposes a ranking exercise using prostitution, obsessive celebrity fantasy, and an AI wife, and one student answers that the AI-wife case is worst because it requires the least will and least real action.

speaker_notes.note: This is a substantive student clarification question about Jiang's model, so it may contribute to the public questions list later if Jiang's answer is retained.
The student answer is exploratory and fragmented but clearly endorses the AI-wife example as the worst case because it expresses minimal will and action.

claims.claim: Jiang argues that lust, gluttony, greed, and wrath are things you do to yourself, while violence, fraud, and treachery are things you do to other people.
The deeper sins matter because they disrupt another person's capacity to live a good life.
Jiang says Dante transforms the usual seven-deadly-sins logic by making lust, gluttony, greed, and wrath into signs of too little ego, will, and hope rather than too much.
A student's formulation that ego, free will, and imagination form a spectrum is accepted by Jiang as a valid way to understand his model.
Jiang interprets Francesca's lust as falling in love with an idea or romance plot rather than with a real person.
Jiang compares Francesca's story to Madame Bovary to emphasize lust as escapist fantasy produced by reading and projection.
In Jiang's contrast, paying for sex expresses ego and money power, while Francesca-style lust expresses insufficient will and a retreat into fantasy.
Jiang uses three examples — paying a prostitute, writing lifelong love letters to a celebrity, and buying an AI wife — as a classroom test for ranking lust by Dante's standards.
One student argues that the AI-wife case is worst because it requires the least strong will and the least real action, while paying for sex at least involves concrete action.

signature_moments.moment: The early circles of Hell are reinterpreted as signs of not enough ego, not too much.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's decisive reversal and a core Jiang move for reading Dante against conventional moral categories.

signature_moments.moment: A student compresses Jiang's whole framework into a single image: ego, free will, and imagination form a spectrum.
signature_moments.source_phrase: ego free will imagination is a spectrum
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives a compact primitive for organizing Jiang's Paradise/Inferno contrast.

signature_moments.moment: Francesca's lust is recast as loving an idea instead of a person.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you are falling in love with an idea as opposed to a person
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns lust into imaginative self-escape rather than simple bodily appetite.

signature_moments.moment: The AI-wife thought experiment modernizes Dante by making despair, fantasy, and passivity visible in contemporary technological form.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you buy yourself an AI wife
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the lecture's sharpest modern bridge between medieval sin and present-day substitutes for real love.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's formula for lust, gluttony, greed, and wrath as failures of will and hope rather than excesses of desire.
Lust as projection into fantasy or romance narrative rather than real love of a person.
Student shorthand, accepted by Jiang, for the continuum linking positive spiritual agency to its degraded forms.

chronology_notes.note: This 2026-06-23 class explicitly updates Dante interpretation by translating the lust problem into modern cases like celebrity obsession and an AI wife.

uncertainty_notes.note: The ASR around 'Madame Bovary' is noisy ('by by um um but yes'), but the literary reference is clear from context.
